This article is pure fear-mongering. They are correct that it is impossible to program in every possible scenario you might encounter on the road, but there are two fundamental problems with that objection:

  1. It assumes that human drivers make the correct decisions in these situations (a very bad assumption)
  2. It assumes that machine learning can't cope with the complexities of driving (also a very bad assumption, especially as our data regarding driving behaviors grows)

For those of you who don't know, machine learning involves using a computer to evaluate a known set of quantifiable inputs and assign a judgment as an output. It works by providing a set of data with known results, then allowing the computer to train using that data until it can provide reasonable approximations on similar data sets where the results are not known. Obviously, the more training data you have, the better your results will be.

This is how Netflix recommends movies: they look at your ratings, what you have watched recently, and compares you to similar people to make suggestions (this is a very rough approximation of the process).

Netflix works with very limited data sets and tries to make recommendations out of a set of movies you have not seen. You have rated what, 100 movies, maybe? They then need to pick out of the tens of thousands you haven't rated. Success is bound to be low.

Automated driving, on the other hand has a distinct advantage: the data sets are rich and only growing richer. More situations are encountered daily and get incorporated into the training set for machine learning. Unlike humans who can only learn from what they see, we can unite data sets from all automated cars. Before long, there will be few situations we do not have data on, and those are unlikely to be familiar to human drivers either. Furthermore, there are a very limited set of responses a car can make: stop, slow down, speed up, turn, and/or combine those options. Given rich training data and a limited set of responses, it is very easy to see computers being able to very quickly judge what the safest response to any emergent road situation is. On top of that, computers never get distracted, never lose focus, never get drunk, and never panic. Given these enormous advantages, it is hard to see automated driving NOT becoming mandatory.

After all this, it is important to remember that machine learning isn't perfect. Inevitably computers will guess wrong, fail, crash, etc. But humans do all this and more at far greater rates. We don't need automated cars to be perfect to be valuable, we just need them to be better than human drivers, and anybody who has fought rush hour traffic knows that is a pretty low bar.
